w:r.w:t: Automated Step Noise Detection for TDD Baseline Files

The Step Noise Finder is a standalone desktop application that automatically scans all channels in one or more TDD baseline files and identifies regions containing periodic step noise. It is designed for Nabsys HD-Mapping instruments that produce multi-channel voltage data (typically 256 channels at 100 Hz).

Step noise is a characteristic interference pattern where the signal abruptly rises, holds at an elevated level, then falls back in a repeating periodic pattern. The application detects step noise in the 4–20 Hz frequency range with configurable amplitude thresholds.
Python 3.11+ with NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib
Or the standalone StepNoiseFinder.exe (no Python required)
Minimum 4 GB RAM (8 GB recommended for batch scanning)
The application window is divided into four areas:
The File menu provides three commands:

The toolbar displays the loaded file information and detection parameters:

After scanning, each row represents a contiguous time segment where step noise was detected. The table columns are:
Filename (truncated) of the source TDD file.
Channel ID (physical channel number, sorted numerically).

Maximum peak-to-peak amplitude of the bandpass-filtered signal in the segment (millivolts).
Pre-baseline: the highest raw signal value in the 10-second window immediately before the step noise starts.

Click any row to view the waveform plots in the right panel.
When a result row is selected, two plots are displayed:

Raw Signal (top): The unfiltered channel voltage in millivolts. The detected step noise region is highlighted in red. Green and orange dashed lines show the pre-baseline and post-baseline values respectively.
Bandpass Filtered (bottom): The signal after bandpass filtering in the configured frequency range, showing the periodic step noise pattern clearly.
Both plots include 5 seconds of context before and after the detected segment. The matplotlib toolbar below the plots provides zoom, pan, and save functionality.
The bottom status bar shows the current application state: file loading status, scan progress summary, or scan completion results (number of segments, channels, and files with detections).
The step noise detection uses a sliding-window approach combining bandpass filtering with autocorrelation analysis:

The raw channel data (in microvolts) is passed through a 2nd-order zero-phase Butterworth bandpass filter. The passband is set slightly wider than the configured frequency range (1 Hz below the low cutoff, 5 Hz above the high cutoff) to avoid edge effects.
The filtered signal is divided into overlapping windows:
Window size: 10 seconds (1000 samples at 100 Hz)
For each window, two tests are applied:
The peak-to-peak amplitude of the filtered signal in the window is computed. If it is below the configured minimum (default 100 mV), the window is skipped. This eliminates quiet segments quickly.
The normalized autocorrelation of the window is computed. The algorithm looks for peaks in the autocorrelation at lags corresponding to the target frequency range:

The peak autocorrelation value in this lag range is the periodicity score. If it exceeds the configured threshold (default 0.4), the window is flagged as containing step noise. The corresponding lag gives the estimated frequency.
Adjacent or overlapping flagged windows are merged into contiguous segments. During merging, the maximum amplitude and periodicity are preserved, and frequencies are averaged.
For each merged segment, the application computes:
Pre-baseline: The maximum raw signal value in the 10-second window immediately before the segment starts.
Post-baseline: The maximum raw signal value in the 10-second window immediately after the segment ends (if data is available).
These baselines help assess whether the step noise is causing a DC offset shift in the channel.

100 mV is typical for Nabsys instruments

4–20 Hz covers most observed step noise

Detect intermittent or irregular step noise
0.4 is a good balance; below 0.3 may produce false positives
The application reads TDD v3.1 binary files produced by Nabsys HD-Mapping instruments. Key details:
Data format: interleaved int16 samples, one per channel per time step
Conversion: raw counts are multiplied by per-channel calibration factors to produce microvolts
Typical files: 256 channels at 100 Hz, 30 minutes of data (~88 MB)
Channel IDs in TDD files are in hardware-scrambled order. The application uses a descrambling function to sort channels numerically (1, 2, 3, …, 256) for display and analysis.

During batch scanning, the application caches loaded file data for plotting. Files without detections are evicted from the cache to conserve memory. Files with detections are retained so their waveforms can be viewed by clicking result rows.
All scanning runs in a background thread to keep the GUI responsive. Progress updates are dispatched to the main thread via tkinter’s after() mechanism.
Matplotlib ≥ 3.7.0 — embedded plots with tkinter backend
